abstract: Heterochiasmy, sex differences in meiotic recombination, is usually described in terms of genetic-map length, potentially obscuring more consequential differences in crossover location. Amphibians provide striking examples of extreme spatial heterochiasmy, with male recombination concentrated near chromosome ends and female recombination broadly distributed, yet the evolution and genetic basis of this pattern remains poorly understood. Here, we combine a review with a phylogenetic comparative synthesis of male chiasma location across 97 amphibian species. Male crossover localization is phylogenetically structured, and ancestral reconstruction favors predominantly interstitial recombination at deeper anuran nodes, although not conclusively. The strongest correlate of male terminal crossover location is chromosome morphology: telocentric-rich karyotypes retain more interstitial male chiasmata, whereas metacentric chromosomes show more terminal male chiasmata. Genome size and sex-chromosome system show little association. We propose a sequential model in which sex-specific meiotic regulation first establishes a crossover-precursor placement bias, while centromere position influences which precursors mature into crossovers. This model predicts that chromosome fusion, fission or centromere repositioning can alter male chiasma location without requiring changes to the underlying meiotic program. Our synthesis highlights crossover location as a distinct dimension of heterochiasmy with consequences for genome-wide linkage, adaptation, divergence and sex-chromosome evolution.
